sentence: This part decides whether one deployment, one copy of a model at an AI provider, may take a request.
Listed teams can have a deployment to themselves for set hours each day.
A team can also own a share of a provisioned deployment, counted in provisioned throughput units (PTUs).
Other callers lose that deployment, and get an error if nothing else is left.
Separately, when an operator turns it on, a per-minute guard counts requests and tokens in each clock minute.
A request over a limit gets 429 Too Many Requests from the router itself, not from the provider.
One flaw costs capacity: a successful call keeps its whole output reservation for the minute, so callers get refused well below the set rate.
During selection, an access-window filter and then a PTU-share filter drop deployments kept for other teams.
When some router in the process lists `enforce_model_rate_limits`, a check then runs on the chosen deployment just before the provider call.
It reserves the request's input estimate against any input-token limit and its maximum output against any output-token limit.
note: Now cites the amounts: [LIMITS-092] 'The ITPM reservation is the estimate when it is positive and `1` otherwise'; [LIMITS-093] max tokens, else the model's listed maximum, else `4096`; [LIMITS-055] (1) the I/O-token reservation 'when the deployment has `itpm` or `otpm`'; [LIMITS-097] each reservation increments its counter and is compared with the limit. The 1-token floor and the explicit-0 skip ([LIMITS-095]) are details the body states.

sentence: It then checks any token and request limits, raising a 429 rate-limit error on a breach.
A failed call refunds its reservation; a successful router call keeps it until the counter expires, because the success event never finds the reservation note.
access window: a daily local-time interval during which a deployment serves only the teams it lists
PTU share: a team's whole number of provisioned throughput units in one shared deployment
per-minute check: the optional check that enforces a deployment's per-minute limits just before the provider call
reservation: tokens a request books against the input and output limits before the call
input-token limit: the most input tokens a deployment takes in one clock minute
output-token limit: the most output tokens a deployment takes in one clock minute
token limit: the most total tokens a deployment takes in one clock minute
note: 'counted after each call' is gone. What remains defines the setting, as for the sibling input, output and request rows: [LIMITS-054] reads `tpm` as the deployment's limit (configuration table: 'per-minute total-token ... ceilings'); [LIMITS-056] refuses once the current minute's usage reaches it. The looseness of enforcement ([LIMITS-172] 'bounds new admissions, not tokens in flight'; [LIMITS-204]/[LIMITS-205] streaming and Anthropic-messages calls never count) is stated in the body and Watch out, not denied here.

sentence: request limit: the most requests a deployment takes in one clock minute
counter: a number in the router's cache for one deployment, one limit and one UTC minute, written with a 60-second expiry
rate-limit error: the error a refused request gets, with status 429
refund: taking a reservation back off its counters and clearing its note
success event: the logging step that runs after a call succeeds and counts its tokens
note: Only 'callback' became 'step'. [LIMITS-066] 'On a success event ...'; [LIMITS-067] TPM tracking increments the tpm counter by `total_tokens`. The skip for events with no model name ([LIMITS-067], [LIMITS-204]) is stated in the body; this row names the step's role and does not say every call is counted.

sentence: failure event: the logging step that runs after a call fails
note: Only 'callback' became 'step'. [LIMITS-069] 'On a failure event the check refunds any I/O reservation ...'.

sentence: reservation note: four bookkeeping entries in the request's metadata that record each reserved amount and its counter
reconcile: correcting a reservation to the tokens the call really used
reserved-deployment error: the error a caller gets when the team filters leave no deployment
team ceiling: the tokens per minute a team's shares buy on one model group
sizing row: the Azure capacity entry giving the input tokens per minute that one provisioned throughput unit buys
settings section: one of a deployment's two sections, provider-call settings or descriptive information; a limit can sit in either, or at the deployment's top level
error category: a label on a rate-limit error that tells a provider's limit from the router's own
request slot: a per-task holder through which the check reads the request it guards
deployment bind: the moment the router attaches a chosen deployment to a request, before each attempt
metadata: the caller's dict of request bookkeeping, which the router writes into in place
Redis: an optional shared store for the router's counters, so every server sees the same counts; without it, each process counts in its own memory
asynchronous call: a router call in the non-blocking style, where the server keeps serving other requests while it waits; the check runs its async methods for it
synchronous call: a router call in the blocking style, where the caller waits for the answer; the check runs its plain methods for it
usage-based routing: a routing strategy that reads and writes the same minute counters to pick a deployment
input-token headers: response headers reporting a group's input-token limit, what remains and when the minute resets; output-token headers do the same for output
When no router in the process lists `enforce_model_rate_limits`, this module enforces no per-minute limit; the team filters still run.
When a deployment sets none of `tpm`, `rpm`, `itpm`, `otpm`, the check passes it unchanged.
When this minute's recorded tokens are at or above `tpm`, refusal with 429 and retry-after 60.
When the count, with this request added, exceeds `rpm`, refusal; the count keeps this request.
When a reservation lifts its counter above `itpm` or `otpm`, the check takes it back, and on an output refusal the input one too.
When the request sets max tokens to 0, no output reservation and no output check.
When an admitted router call fails, its reservations come back; token and request counts stay.
When an admitted router call succeeds, no reconcile; its reservations stay until their counters expire.
When anything else raises in the check, such as a null settings section, the check admits and skips the remaining steps; no cooldown follows.
When the deployment lacks an id or a provider model, no reservation; input and output limits go unenforced.
When every candidate falls to an active window that omits the caller's team, `litellm.BadRequestError` with the window's end time and zone.
When the caller's team holds a share on some candidate, only shared candidates naming that team stay; other callers, the master key and no-team callers included, keep only open ones.
When a router loads a model list with malformed windows, an error naming the model, or, when the router ignores invalid deployments, a log line and a skip.
An access window keeps a deployment for listed teams during a daily stretch of local time.
While a window is active, a caller from an unlisted team, or with no team, loses that deployment.
If no deployment is left, the caller gets an error saying when the window ends.
Windows sit in `model_info.access_windows`, each with start, end, time zone and teams.
The filter turns the current UTC instant into that zone and compares only the time of day, start included and end excluded.
A 22:00 to 06:00 window crosses midnight, so it is active at 22:00 and not at 06:00.
A team listed only in an inactive window counts as unlisted; a deployment with no active window stays for everyone.

When the filter drops every candidate, selection raises `litellm.BadRequestError` with a message such as `"Deployment g is reserved for another team until 02:07 UTC"`, and a chat call appends its fallback outcome note.
A provisioned deployment can split its units among teams as shares.
If the caller's team holds a share on any deployment that could serve the request, it keeps only the shared ones naming it; otherwise it keeps only deployments with no shares.
Where capacity is known, shares also set a team ceiling on tokens per minute, which the proxy enforces.
The map sits in `model_info.ptu_shares`; one invalid entry makes the whole map count as absent, and a valid map is the access rule even without pricing terms.
A single-team deployment counts as open here; in a shared group, the router's separate team lookup withholds it from other teams but offers it to a caller with no team.
When the filter drops candidates and keeps none, the router raises `litellm.BadRequestError` saying the deployment is reserved for the teams holding a PTU share of it.
The team ceiling sums each share times the sizing row's `input_tpm_per_ptu` over the group's sized, shared deployments naming the team.
The sizing row comes from the Azure capacity table, matched on `model_info.base_model` first, then on the provider model string.
When switched on, a per-minute check looks at the chosen deployment just before the provider call.
It reserves tokens against any input and output limits, then checks any total-token and request limits; the first limit hit refuses with the router's own 429.
A router creates the check only when its `optional_pre_call_checks` list `enforce_model_rate_limits`.
It builds one `ModelRateLimitingCheck` over its own cache and adds it to a process-wide callback list, unless one is already there.
Routers run every check on that list, so one registration guards every router in the process, all counting in the first router's cache.
Each limit is the first set value among the deployment's top level, `litellm_params` and `model_info`, and 0 counts as set.
The token limit only reads its counter, because the success event adds tokens after the call.
So with no usage recorded even a token limit of 0 admits, and concurrent requests can together pass the limit.
The request limit adds 1 first and refuses above the limit, so with a limit of 2 and four concurrent requests on one process, exactly two pass.

Every refusal raises `litellm.RateLimitError` with a retry-after header of 60 seconds and text such as `"litellm.RateLimitError: Model rate limit exceeded. TPM limit=1000, current usage=1000"`, to which the router appends an outcome note when it re-raises.
Its `category` is the default `vendor_rate_limit`.
The async dispatcher hands the refused deployment to the cooldown handler with status 429; failure-handling decides whether it cools down.
Last check before the call: When switched on, the check sees the chosen deployment just before the provider call.
Tokens come first: A deployment with an input-token limit first reserves the request's estimated input, and one with an output-token limit reserves its maximum output.
An overflow undoes itself: A reservation that pushes a counter over its limit comes straight back off, and the request gets a 429.
No limits, no counting: A deployment with neither a token nor a request limit goes on to the provider.
The token limit only looks: The token limit refuses once the minute's recorded tokens reach it; it adds nothing before the call.
The request limit counts first: The request limit adds this request, then refuses above the limit, and the refused request stays in the count.
Errors let requests through: Any other error inside the check lets the deployment through and skips the remaining steps, leaving only a debug log line.
In the usual case, an input token limit makes a request reserve a guess at its input, and an output token limit the most output it allows.
A reservation that would pass its limit comes straight back off, and the check refuses.
On the normal call path, the router fills the check's request slot at every deployment bind, but only for deployments with input or output limits.
The router's turn-admission path strips those two limits first, so it never reserves.
The input reservation is the tokenizer's count of the messages or prompt, or 1 token when that count is 0 or fails.
The output reservation is the request's max tokens, else the model's listed maximum, else 4096; an explicit 0 skips it and its check.
Nothing caps a reservation, so the check always refuses a request whose reservation alone exceeds its limit.
Each reservation adds its amount to the counter, then compares; above the limit it subtracts the whole amount again and raises, while landing exactly on the limit passes.
With an output limit of 10, max tokens of 4 and eight concurrent requests, exactly two pass.
When the reservations fit, the check writes a reservation note into the request's `metadata`, which through the router's chat calls is the caller's own dict.
If the slot holds no request, the counters still grow but no note exists, so nothing refunds that reservation before its counter expires.
The reservations fit: For each input or output limit that is set, the check adds the input estimate or the maximum output to this minute's counter, then writes a note into the request.
note: Now cites each part: amounts [LIMITS-092] (estimate, floored at 1) and [LIMITS-093] (max tokens); per-minute counter [LIMITS-089] (key with UTC hour and minute); increment by the reserved amount [LIMITS-097]; 'After both reservations succeed, the four sentinels are written into the slot kwargs' [LIMITS-100]. The no-note case of an empty slot ([LIMITS-101]) is told in the prose just above the figure.

sentence: Trouble gives tokens back: A failed call, a token or request refusal in the same check, or the next deployment bind subtracts the reserved amounts and clears the note.
Success keeps everything: The router's success event never finds the note, so the whole reservation stays until the minute's counter expires.
Correction needs the note: Only a success event that carries the note where the check looks, with a usage count, corrects the counters to real use.
A failed call gives its reserved tokens back.
A successful call through the router does not: its whole reservation stays on the counters until they expire, even when the reply used far fewer tokens.
A failure event refunds the reserved amounts and clears the note, but never touches the token or request counters.
A token or request refusal in the same check also refunds, when the slot holds the request that reserved.
So does the next deployment bind of any request carrying a note, including a later request that reuses the caller's dict; that refund trusts forged notes too.
The success event reconciles only when it finds the note in the callback's top-level `metadata` or the standard logging object's metadata.
The router's success events carry it in neither place, so the router never reconciles a successful call.
A success event that does carry the note there corrects each counter by actual minus reserved, provided it finds the call's usage.
The success event also adds total tokens to the token counter, but skips events with no model name.
So the router's streaming chat and Anthropic-messages calls never count toward the token limit.
If the model name it writes under ever differs from the provider model the check reads, the token limit never applies.
In the example, deployment D's output limit is 50, and the clock starts on a UTC minute.
Had the router reconciled A, the counter would have read 5, leaving room for B.
0s, Request A: asks for up to 40 tokens; admitted
0s, Output counter: rises by 40; 40 of 50
10s, Request A: succeeds after 5 output tokens; done
10s, Output counter: no correction for A; still 40 of 50
20s, Request B: asks for up to 40 tokens; refused with 429
20s, Output counter: briefly 80, then back down; 40 of 50
60s, Output counter: next UTC minute begins; fresh counter
61s, Request B: caller sends it again; admitted
61s, Output counter: rises by 40; 40 of 50
Each limit counts one fixed clock minute in UTC, then starts a fresh count.
While a shared Redis store works, the request and reservation limits count the traffic of every server.
Without Redis, each process counts alone.
A counter key holds the deployment id, provider model and UTC hour and minute, such as `"global_router:d1:gpt-4o:itpm:01-36"`, and every write carries a 60-second expiry.
A group's remaining-usage response gains input-token headers only with an input limit, output-token ones only with an output limit.
A successful router call keeps its whole token reservation for the minute, so callers see output-limit refusals well below the set rate.
Streaming chat calls and Anthropic messages calls never count toward a deployment's token limit, so that limit does not bound them.
On every router, a caller can forge a reservation note that lowers another deployment's counter; a forged 1-token refund per request keeps a 1-request-a-minute deployment admitting without end.

The check fails open: a null settings section, or max-tokens text such as "abc" on an input- or output-limited deployment, lets the request through with every limit off. Only a debug log line records it.
These refusals carry a provider's rate-limit label, so clients that sort errors by source blame the provider for the router's own limit.
If Redis fails, two servers, each counting alone, admit up to twice the limit on an asynchronous call.
note: [LIMITS-142]: 'the async check compares this replica's own in-memory count ([LIMITS-121]), so each replica enforces the limit on its own traffic and N replicas together admit up to N times the limit', with the example of one request admitted on each of two async replicas. The token limit is also judged on the local value when the Redis read fails ([LIMITS-057], [LIMITS-058]), so the statement holds for it too.

sentence: A synchronous call then skips request, input-token and output-token limits.
note: Now scoped to the incremented limits, as [LIMITS-142] says: 'the sync check's increment re-raises and the request is admitted with no RPM, ITPM or OTPM limit at all ([LIMITS-064])'; [LIMITS-121] 'A sync counter increment re-raises cache errors'. It no longer claims the token limit is skipped (that limit can still refuse on the local value, [LIMITS-057]). Code check: `DualCache.increment_cache` and `RedisCache.increment_cache` re-raise.

sentence: With the usage-based routing strategy (version 2) also on, each request counts twice, so a limit of 4 requests a minute admits only 2.
A broken share map counts as no share, and deployments added while the router runs skip the check that refuses one, so an empty share map serves every team.
